source_text: Sic enim et in Evangelio suo dixerat: Mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit [n38] ; non utique ut elementa Christum ratione carentia potuisse viderentur vel cognoscere vel negare; sed ut mundi appellatione turba infidelium signaretur. Eodem ergo more in praesenti quoque, omne quod in mundo est, id est, omnia genera hominum ita voluptatibus inhaerentia, ut bona cuncta rationabilis animantis aut potestatum phaleris, aut opum sarcinis, sensibus metiantur, exosa ait superbia turguisse, quae ex Deo non est, id est, Deo non placet, sed ex mundo est, voluntatis scilicet humanae pravitate concepta. Et ideo vos, inquit, sua non debet aemulatione corrumpere; quia qui facit voluntatem Dei, aeternae fit beatitudinis compos, nec cum praesentium fragilitate praetervolat. Ergo Ioannes apostolus odio haberi mundum praecepit, quomodo et Dominus in Evangelio, non solum corpus, sed etiam animam ipsam nostram odio habendam esse monstravit: Qui - inquit - non odit patrem, aut fratrem, insuper etiam animam suam, non est me dignus [n39] . Cum certe fidelium animus se odisse non possit, qui amore consultissimo felicitatem suam doloribus etiam et periculis mercatur. Quid igitur egimus? Apostolum videlicet Ioannem, ex more Scripturarum mundi vocabulo non naturam perculisse rerum, sed vitia voluntatum; atque ita concupiscentiam carnis negasse ex Deo esse, sicut omnia quae in mundo sunt. Quod Manichaeus non secundum Apostoli sensum, sed secundum perfidiam suam velut consequenter arripiens, non concupiscentiam carnis, nec ipsam carnem, nec totum postremo mundum a Deo confirmat effectum; quem tu secutus, concupiscentiam carnis, non a Deo, sed a diabolo conditam credis.
pass_a_gloss: For thus he had also said in his Gospel: The world was made through him, and the world did not know him; not, that is, so that the elements lacking reason might seem to have been able either to know or to deny Christ; but so that by the appellation of the world the crowd of unbelievers might be marked. In the same manner therefore also in the present, everything that is in the world, that is, all kinds of humans so clinging to pleasures that they measure all goods of a rational living being either by the trappings of powers or by the burdens of wealth, by the senses, he says has swollen with hateful pride, which is not from God, that is, does not please God, but is from the world, conceived namely by the crookedness of human will. And therefore, he says, it ought not to corrupt you by its rivalry; because he who does the will of God is made possessor of eternal blessedness, and does not fly past with the fragility of present things. Therefore John the apostle commanded the world to be held in hatred, just as also the Lord in the Gospel showed that not only the body but even our very soul is to be held in hatred: He who — he says — does not hate father, or brother, and moreover even his own soul, is not worthy of me. When certainly the mind of the faithful cannot hate itself, which by most considered love buys its own happiness even with pains and dangers. What therefore have we done? Namely we have shown that the Apostle John, from the custom of the Scriptures, by the word of the world struck not the nature of things but the vices of wills; and thus denied that the desire of the flesh is from God, just as all things which are in the world. Which Manichaeus, snatching not according to the Apostle's sense but according to his own treachery as if consequently, confirms that not the desire of the flesh, nor the flesh itself, nor finally the whole world was made by God; whom you, having followed, believe that the desire of the flesh was founded not by God but by the devil.

pass_b_english: For he had also said in his Gospel: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:10) (Matthew 10:37). He certainly did not mean that the elements, which lack reason, could appear capable of knowing or denying Christ. He meant the multitude of unbelievers to be designated by the name “world.” In the same way here, too, he says that everything in the world—that is, every sort of person so devoted to pleasures that they measure all the goods of a rational creature by the trappings of power, loads of wealth, or the senses—has swollen with hateful pride. This is not from God, meaning it does not please God, but is from the world: it is conceived through the perversity of the human will. “Therefore,” he says in effect, “it must not corrupt you by making you imitate it. Whoever does God’s will comes to share eternal blessedness and does not fly past with the frailty of present things.”

So the apostle John commanded the world to be hated in the same way that the Lord in the Gospel showed that not only our body but even our soul itself must be hated: “Whoever does not hate father or brother, and even his own soul as well, is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:26; compare Matthew 10:37). Yet the mind of a believer certainly cannot hate itself when, out of the most thoughtful love, it purchases its own happiness even through pains and dangers. What, then, have we established? That the apostle John, following Scripture’s custom, struck with the word “world” not the nature of things but the vices of wills. And he denied that the desire of the flesh is from God in the same way that he denied this of everything in the world. Manichaeus seized on this, as though following its logic, but according to his own faithlessness rather than the apostle’s meaning. He asserts that neither the desire of the flesh, nor flesh itself, nor, finally, the whole world was made by God. Following him, you believe that the desire of the flesh was created not by God but by the devil.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
